market_context: United States/Canada; household recognition of termite signs and structural prevention with professional inspection rather than DIY chemical treatment instructions.
title: How to Tell If You Have Termites at Home

seo.title: How to Tell If You Have Termites: Key Signs
seo.meta_description: Look for discarded wings, mud tubes, hollow or damaged wood and swarms. Learn how termites differ from ants and when to get a professional inspection.
seo.search_intent: Recognize signs consistent with termites, distinguish them from other insects and know when a home needs professional inspection.

excerpt: Useful termite signs include swarms of winged insects, discarded wings near windows, mud tubes on foundations or walls, and wood that sounds hollow or shows internal galleries. Not all damaged wood has termites and not every winged insect is a termite. When several signs line up—especially around structural wood—get a professional inspection before attempting treatment.
content_html:
Termites often stay unnoticed because much of their activity takes place inside wood, soil or protected tunnels. That means the first sign is not always a room full of insects. It may be a pile of wings by a window, a narrow mud line on the foundation or wood that looks normal outside but has been hollowed internally.

A homeowner inspection does not need to identify the exact species with certainty. Its job is to recognize a pattern that deserves professional inspection.

Swarms are one of the most visible clues

EPA notes that many people first discover termites when a reproductive swarm appears. Winged termites emerge seasonally and may collect near windows, doors or lights.

Afterward, piles of detached wings can remain on sills or floors. Several similar wings in the same location are worth documenting.

Do not confuse winged termites with winged ants

EPA gives useful distinctions: termites generally have straight antennae and front and rear wings of roughly equal length, while ants have elbowed antennae and larger front wings.

A clear photograph or securely contained specimen can help with expert identification. You do not need to crush the insect to examine it.

Mud tubes are an important clue for subterranean termites

Look for narrow earthen tubes traveling up foundations, piers, basement walls or other locations where wood is accessible from soil. Subterranean termites use these protected routes between the colony and food.

Do not break every tube simply to see what happens. Photograph the location and preserve the evidence for an inspector who can judge activity and access points.

Wood can look intact while being damaged inside

EPA suggests examining exposed wood for hollow areas. Gentle tapping or careful probing of already suspicious exposed wood may reveal a problem, but do not damage structural components or finishes for a DIY investigation.

Soft wood, a thin intact surface over galleries or unusual internal channels all justify attention, although moisture damage and other wood-destroying insects can look different.

Look at moisture and soil-to-wood conditions

Leaks, poor drainage and wood close to soil can make a structure more vulnerable. EPA recommends keeping the foundation area dry, repairing leaks and avoiding wood debris piled beside the building.

Those conditions do not prove termites, but they help explain why one location deserves closer inspection.

Inspect transition points in the structure

Utility penetrations, foundation cracks, porches, low wood trim, basements, crawl spaces and wood-to-masonry transitions are reasonable places for a visual check.

Do not remove siding or drill walls without a clear reason. Hidden termite activity requires a methodical inspection, not random destructive searching.

Damage may be old rather than active

Finding damaged wood does not automatically prove current activity. A house may contain repaired or abandoned damage from a previous infestation.

Separating historic damage from active termites is one reason structural evidence is best evaluated professionally.

Do not turn a suspicion into a DIY chemical treatment

EPA warns that termite treatments—especially soil-applied barriers—must be installed correctly to avoid contamination and failure. Many require trained, licensed pest professionals.

The practical priority is risk identification, moisture and access correction, and qualified evaluation rather than improvised extermination.

What you can do preventively while arranging inspection

Repair leaks, gutters and drainage that keep the foundation wet. Move firewood and wood debris away from the structure and prevent plants from growing against exposed wood.

Seal appropriate foundation cracks and utility penetrations as part of normal building maintenance.

When to arrange inspection promptly

Call when you find mud tubes, indoor swarms, repeated piles of wings, structural wood damage or several compatible clues in the same area.

A termite inspection can also be worthwhile before purchasing a home in a termite-prone region or when the building has a known history.

The pattern matters more than one isolated clue

One wing can blow indoors. One crack can be ordinary. Wings, tubes, moisture and wood damage together tell a very different story.

The best response to suspected termites is not to apply something immediately; it is to confirm what is happening before a hidden structural problem continues.

faq.question: What are common signs of termites?
faq.answer: Swarms, discarded wings, mud tubes and wood with hollow areas or internal galleries are common signs.

faq.question: How can I tell a winged termite from a winged ant?
faq.answer: Termites generally have straight antennae and similar-length wings; ants have elbowed antennae and larger front wings.

faq.question: Should I break mud tubes to see if they are active?
faq.answer: There is no need to destroy all evidence. Photograph the tubes and have an inspector evaluate activity and the surrounding structure.

faq.question: Can I treat termites myself?
faq.answer: Structural termite treatments require correct application and often licensed professionals. Confirm the problem first and use a qualified inspector or pest professional.
